newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine deputy PM bemoans IMF standby offer.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine deputy PM bemoans IMF standby offer.

text.p: Ukraine's energetic deputy prime minister in charge of reforms lost his usual equanimity on Thursday after it became clear his former Soviet republic had failed to win a quick decision on a multi-billion-dollar loan.

Serhiy Tyhypko was clearly upset at a news conference after the International Monetary Fund said it was considering an interim standby deal instead of a three-year, $2.5-$3 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF).

"Don't torment me now about the standby. I am not ready for this. I still want the EFF," said Tyhypko, a young banker brought in by President Leonid Kuchma after his predecessor quit in disgust at the attitude of parliament and government.
"For me personally the standby issue is a serious defeat," said Tyhypko, who has been trying to push parliament into passing last-minute laws as it prepares to recess on July 18.
"We did so much recently to extract the EFF, and each time we did something, we devised, we schemed, and we didn't get it through parliament," he added.

Tyhpko said the main sticking point with the IMF, whose mission ended on Thursday saying it would come back from July 21 to 27 to discuss a standby credit, had been failure to approve tax reforms underpinning this year's budget.

Parliament passed the document only on June 27 -- almost six months late -- and Kuchma has proposed postponing an election due in March 1988 by one year to give the conservative-dominated chamber more time to swallow reforms.
Tyhypko, 38, headed Privatbank, one of Ukraine's most successful, until his appointment, which surprised many analysts who noted he had no government experience.

Since then he has conducted a visible campaign for reforms, appearing at government seminars on television with his collar unbuttoned and clutching a notepad and pen as the clock ticked on Ukraine's hopes for the EFF and timely passage of the budget.
Tyhypko said a second standby like one which expired in February was needed while Ukraine approved an outstanding seven or eight items on the Fund's 41-item wish list.
For the IMF, meeting all the items on the list would have proved Ukraine was undertaking structural reforms.
Tyhypko said Kuchma would keep working on the EFF and keep talking to the IMF, whose last standby deal worth $867 million with Ukraine was signed in May 1996.
He gave no forecast for the size of the interim loan, saying only that it "could be half the size of the EFF".
He added that government was actively preparing for a key cabinet meeting on July 24, a week after the first meeting of a presidential council that would take economic decisions.
"We will try to come up with a concrete, constructive programme, which would help us solve social problems and really rationalise our activities," he said.

Adalbert Knobl, IMF mission chief to Ukraine, told Reuters a standby deal was being considered pending key reforms including lowering payroll taxes to 40 percent from 53 percent, charging 100 percent for communal services, and removal of privileges such as free bus rides for sectors of society.

Knobl said the standby could be approved by the end of August, and the EFF could be issued by the end of the year or early 1998. "In the meantime, we will continue to work with the government to be able to move to an EFF as soon as possible," the Fund said in a statement.
